newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japanese 97 growth to slow, then accelerate - OECD.
newsitem.headline: Japanese 97 growth to slow, then accelerate - OECD.

text.p: Japan's economic recovery may stagger from the impact of higher taxes in 1997, but will accelerate once again the following year as the economy enters a period of expansion, the Organisation for Economic Cooperation and Development (OECD) said on Thursday.

In its half-yearly economic report, the Paris-based think tank predicted Japan's real gross domestic product (GDP) will grow by 1.6 percent in 1997 and 3.7 percent in 1998, after 3.6 percent growth in 1996.
The OECD had forecast 2.2 percent GDP growth in 1996 and 2.4 percent in 1997 in its previous report in June.

"With increases in personal incomes, the slower rise in import prices and the continued expansion of business investment helping to offset the damping effect on demand of the planned fiscal tightening, the recovery is projected to regain momentum during 1997," the report said.

"In addition, the yen depreciation should reverse the drag on activity from the foreign sector...for 1997 as a whole, with the fiscal consolidation assumed, growth may reach only (about) one and a half percent before accelerating once again in 1998."
A sharp decline in public works spending and expected tax increases may slow domestic demand in 1997, it said.

But growth is expected to pick up in the second half of 1997 and rise further in 1988, with business investment continuing to lead the overall recovery and the drag from net exports diminishing sharply with the lower yen exchange rate.

The OECD said that the continuation of the recovery will depend on whether there will be enough acceleration in private sector demand to offset an easing of public sector spending which had supported the recovery in the past year.
Fiscal policy is likely to be tightened with steps to reduce government deficits, such as a consumption tax hike and an expected end to special income tax cuts from January 1997.
These are expected to reduce growth of real disposable incomes, the OECD said.
"In Japan and much of the European Union, however, the pace of fiscal consolidation in the near term must also reflect the need to nurture a nascent economic recovery," the report said.

As a way to prevent a serious economic setback, the OECD said the monetary authorities will need to maintain an easy policy stance for "some time to come", a measure which has helped the economic recovery so far.
Japanese OECD chief economist Kumiharu Shigehara, a former central banker, told a news conference official interest rates were low in Japan and should stay low.
"It (Japan) should maintain the current low level while embarking on fiscal consolidation," Shigehara said.
Company profits have been helped by lower interest rates, higher export prices and continued restructuring, leading to a boost in corporate capital investment.
The fall in interest rates has also helped major banks to rebuild their capital base -- eroded by non-performing loans -- by boosting operating profits, the report said.
If continued, easy monetary policy would help improve the balance sheets of the financial sector further and ensure that the banking sector provides enough liquidity to the economy.
The weaker yen will be another force sustaining the recovery, the report said.
The current account surplus is seen stabilising at 1.4 percent of GDP in 1997 and 1.5 percent in 1998.
Further depreciation of the yen might accentuate a fall in personal savings and would also boost business profits and investment more strongly.

A renewed yen appreciation, on the other hand, could encourage firms to accelerate a shift of production overseas, with declining exports and slow growth worsening labour market conditions in the short term.

Inflation will be negligible, despite a rise in the consumption tax, which will lift prices by about one percentage point in 1997. The OECD sees inflation up 0.5 percent in 1997, and unchanged in 1998, after a 0.1 percent decline n 1996.
The jobless rate is likely to ease to 3.2 percent in 1997 and 3.1 percent in 1998, versus 3.3 percent in 1996.
